title: Python Programming Foundations

target.learner: A tertiary fresher or independent beginner with basic computer literacy and no assumed programming experience
target.professionalOutcome: Write, run, debug, test, document, and publish small dependency-free Python programs with enough fluency for introductory practical examinations and beginner projects.

assumptions: The learner has a Windows computer and basic file, browser, and typing skills.
No prior programming, command-line, Git, Python, testing, or object-oriented knowledge is assumed.
Setup is separate from the eight instructional Weeks and may be skipped capability by capability after verification.
Required learning resources are free to access; a free verified GitHub account is needed only for final repository publication.
Most project work can continue offline after the required tools and referenced materials have been opened or downloaded.

competencies.name: Prepare and verify a Python workspace
competencies.description: Create a project folder, edit a Python file in VS Code, select the intended interpreter, and run it from PowerShell.

competencies.name: Run scripts and communicate with text
competencies.description: Use print, input, strings, numeric conversion, and formatted strings in a repeatable saved program.

competencies.name: Read and repair an early Python failure
competencies.description: Use the command, traceback, exception type, line, and caret to repair a wrong path, syntax error, name error, or indentation error.

competencies.name: Represent and calculate with Python values
competencies.description: Use readable variables, integers, floats, strings, Booleans, arithmetic operators, precedence, and explicit conversion.

competencies.name: Express ordered decisions
competencies.description: Use comparisons, Boolean operators, and if/elif/else in an order that produces one explainable result.

competencies.name: Recover from invalid numeric input
competencies.description: Use try/except ValueError around the smallest conversion boundary without hiding unrelated defects.

competencies.name: Repeat until a condition changes
competencies.description: Use while, a deliberate state update, break, and a defensible loop condition without creating an accidental infinite loop.

competencies.name: Process ordered data with lists and for loops
competencies.description: Create, index, update, append, and traverse a list while respecting zero-based boundaries.

competencies.name: Model named records with dictionaries
competencies.description: Create, read, update, test, and iterate dictionary keys and values for understandable records and summaries.

competencies.name: Define and call focused functions
competencies.description: Write functions with purposeful names and parameters, then call them with appropriate arguments.

competencies.name: Return and compose useful values
competencies.description: Return values rather than relying on incidental printing, and combine focused functions into a larger calculation.

competencies.name: Reason about local scope and mutation
competencies.description: Distinguish local names from outer names and avoid hidden dependence on mutable global state.

competencies.name: Address files with pathlib
competencies.description: Build a project-relative Path, inspect whether it exists, and avoid depending on an unexplained working-directory assumption.

competencies.name: Read and write text defensively
competencies.description: Use with blocks and explicit UTF-8 encoding while distinguishing a missing file from an existing unreadable or malformed file.

competencies.name: Round-trip JSON data safely
competencies.description: Serialize supported Python data to JSON text and load it back without confusing JSON data with executable Python objects.

competencies.name: Create simple class instances
competencies.description: Define a class initializer, construct independent instances, and distinguish instance attributes from local variables.

competencies.name: Change object state through methods
competencies.description: Write and call a small instance method that validates and changes the intended object without altering unrelated instances.

competencies.name: Separate a program into modules
competencies.description: Import focused functions or classes from local modules and avoid accidentally executing application code during import.

competencies.name: Protect an application entry point
competencies.description: Use a main function and the __name__ guard so a file behaves deliberately when run and when imported.

competencies.name: Verify behavior with unittest
competencies.description: Write deterministic tests with assertEqual, assertRaises, and isolated temporary data for normal, boundary, and invalid behavior.

competencies.name: Inspect a failing case with the debugger
competencies.description: Set a breakpoint, step through one failing case, inspect local values, repair one cause, and rerun the same test.

competencies.name: Parse a small command-line interface
competencies.description: Use argparse to define commands or options, validate supplied values, and provide usable help without hand-parsing fragile strings.

competencies.name: Document and publish a safe Git repository
competencies.description: Write reproducible setup, run, and test instructions, inspect staged paths, commit locally, and push a secret-free project to GitHub.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A .py file stores instructions; the selected Python interpreter reads and executes them.
concepts.example: `py hello.py` runs the saved file with the Windows Python launcher.
concepts.commonMistake: Expecting a file to run merely because it is open in VS Code.

concepts.simpleMeaning: Python executes the saved file, so an editor change must be saved before the next run.
concepts.example: Change a greeting, save, then repeat the same command.
concepts.commonMistake: Diagnosing old output before checking whether the file was saved.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A traceback names the failing file, line, exception type, and message.
concepts.example: NameError points to a name Python could not find.
concepts.commonMistake: Changing many lines before reading the last traceback entry.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A variable name refers to a value that may be used or replaced later.
concepts.example: `hours = 6` binds the name hours to the integer 6.
concepts.commonMistake: Confusing the name with a quoted string containing that name.

concepts.simpleMeaning: Conversion deliberately produces a different type before an operation.
concepts.commonMistake: Adding numeric-looking text to a number.

concepts.simpleMeaning: An f-string inserts evaluated expressions into labelled text.
concepts.commonMistake: Omitting the f prefix and printing braces literally.

concepts.simpleMeaning: Comparisons and Boolean operators produce True or False for a decision.
concepts.commonMistake: Using = when a comparison requires ==.

concepts.simpleMeaning: if/elif/else checks conditions in order and takes the first matching branch.
concepts.example: Reject invalid data before eligibility rules.
concepts.commonMistake: Placing a broad success condition before a required rejection.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A try block should contain only the operation whose expected failure is being handled.
concepts.commonMistake: Catching Exception around the entire program and hiding defects.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A while loop must have a condition and an action that can move it toward stopping.
concepts.example: Increment attempts after each failed guess.
concepts.commonMistake: Forgetting the update and creating an infinite loop.

concepts.simpleMeaning: List indexes begin at zero while len counts stored values.
concepts.commonMistake: Reading scores[len(scores)] as the last item.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A for loop visits each item in an iterable without manual index arithmetic.
concepts.example: `for score in scores:` processes every stored score.
concepts.commonMistake: Changing list length unexpectedly while traversing it.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A dictionary groups values under meaningful keys.
concepts.commonMistake: Using a positional index for a named field.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A focused function accepts stated inputs and returns or performs one understandable result.
concepts.commonMistake: Making one function collect input, calculate, save, and print everything.

concepts.simpleMeaning: return sends a value to the caller and ends that call.
concepts.example: `return subtotal - discount` lets another function format the result.
concepts.commonMistake: Printing a value when the caller needs to use it.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A name created inside a function is local unless deliberately passed or returned.
concepts.commonMistake: Reading a local name from outside the function.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A Path represents a filesystem location and can be joined without fragile string separators.
concepts.commonMistake: Assuming the terminal always starts in the project folder.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A with block closes an opened file even when an operation fails.
concepts.commonMistake: Leaving files open or relying on a platform-default encoding.

concepts.simpleMeaning: json.dump/load or dumps/loads convert supported Python data to JSON and back.
concepts.example: A list of expense dictionaries can be saved and loaded.
concepts.commonMistake: Expecting JSON to restore class methods or arbitrary Python types.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A class describes construction and behavior; each instance carries its own attributes.
concepts.commonMistake: Using a class attribute when each object needs separate state.

concepts.simpleMeaning: self refers to the instance receiving a method call.
concepts.commonMistake: Omitting self from an instance method definition.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A method can reject an invalid state transition before changing the object.
concepts.example: checkout rejects a book that is already borrowed.
concepts.commonMistake: Changing state first and validating afterward.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A module exposes reusable names while application flow stays in an entry file.
concepts.commonMistake: Creating circular imports or running the CLI during import.

concepts.simpleMeaning: The __name__ guard runs application code only when its file is the entry point.
concepts.commonMistake: Putting tests or user prompts at module top level.

concepts.simpleMeaning: An assertion compares actual behavior with an expected result and reports a mismatch.
concepts.commonMistake: Changing the expected result only to make a test pass.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A breakpoint pauses before a suspicious line so local values and control flow can be inspected.
concepts.example: Pause before a return and inspect the calculated result.
concepts.commonMistake: Adding many prints before reducing the failure to one case.

concepts.simpleMeaning: argparse turns declared command-line choices into validated values and generated help.
concepts.commonMistake: Splitting raw command text by hand and accepting ambiguous input.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A repository is reviewable when its tracked files and README let another person run and test it safely.
concepts.example: README gives exact Python and unittest commands.
concepts.commonMistake: Publishing credentials, private data, caches, or undocumented commands.

questions.prompt: A valid age includes both 16 and 120. Which expression states that rule directly?

questions.prompt: A checker must print exactly one result: invalid, ineligible, or eligible. Why is an `if` followed by `elif` branches useful?

options.label: It stores every result in a dictionary

After one condition matches, later branches in the chain are skipped

questions.prompt: Registration succeeds only when `score >= 50` and `has_prerequisite` is true. Which expression enforces both requirements?
questions.explanation: `and` is true only when both operands are true. `or` would accept someone who meets only one requirement.

questions.prompt: Which handler is appropriately specific when `int(age_text)` receives `"eighteen"`?
questions.explanation: `int` raises ValueError for text that is not a valid integer. Handling that specific expected failure avoids hiding unrelated defects.

questions.prompt: A learner may enter ` YES `. Which expression prepares the answer for comparison with `"yes"`?
questions.explanation: `strip()` removes surrounding spaces and `lower()` normalizes letter case, so ` YES ` becomes `yes`.

questions.prompt: Inside a condition, which expression asks whether `score` is exactly 50?
questions.explanation: `==` compares values. A single `=` is the assignment operator and is not the equality test required here.

questions.prompt: Given age 16, score 50, and a completed prerequisite, what should the supplied inclusive contract decide?

options.label: Reject age because only values above 16 pass
Reject score because only values above 50 pass
Raise ValueError because boundary values are invalid
Accept because both lower boundaries are included

questions.explanation: `16 <= age` and `score >= 50` both include equality. With the prerequisite complete, this boundary case is eligible.

questions.prompt: Why should nonnumeric age text be handled before the age-range comparison?

options.label: It makes the terminal use fewer colors
It changes the answer into a dictionary
A valid number is required before numeric range rules are meaningful
It guarantees every applicant becomes eligible

questions.explanation: Range comparisons require a numeric value. Invalid conversion is a data-quality outcome, not an ordinary under-age decision.

questions.prompt: A try block converts age but also contains a misspelled variable. Why is `except Exception:` around the entire checker harmful here?

options.label: It can disguise the NameError as if the learner merely entered bad data
It prevents Python from comparing integers
It automatically repeats every invalid input

questions.explanation: A broad handler can catch an unrelated programming defect and present a misleading input message. The protected operation should be the expected conversion boundary.

questions.prompt: An if/elif chain first checks `not has_prerequisite`, then `score < 50`. Both are true. Which outcome runs?

options.label: Only the first matching prerequisite branch runs
Only the later score branch runs
The else branch runs because two conditions matched

questions.explanation: In one if/elif chain, Python enters the first true branch and skips the remaining elif and else branches.

It publishes the file to GitHub

It changes a Path into a string

a remains available; b becomes unavailable

builds.brief: Build `tasktrail-cli`. Each record is exactly `{id: int, title: str, course: str, status: "open" | "done"}`; IDs start at 1 and use highest existing ID plus 1. Commands are `add "<title>" --course "<course>"`, `list [--status open|done]`, `complete <id>`, and `--help`. steps.text: Copy the exact record, command, message, and file contracts into README before coding. Run each command on paper and identify which layer owns validation, storage, and output.

Create the project tree. Implement pure `add_task`, `filter_tasks`, and `complete_task` functions with copied lists/records, exact validation errors, stable integer IDs, and no mutation of failed inputs.
Reuse the defensive JSON storage contract: only FileNotFoundError produces an empty list, malformed JSON stops without a write, and a successful add/complete saves once.
Declare argparse subparsers for add, list, and complete. Route parsed values in cli.py, print the supplied output, and keep execution behind main and the __name__ guard.

Write at least eight named tests: first/next ID, blank title/course, open/done filter, unknown status rejected by argparse or pure function as specified, successful complete, unknown ID, repeated complete, and no input mutation.

Run the normal journey, empty list, filtered list, invalid blank add, unknown ID, repeated complete, restart persistence, and malformed-JSON protection cases. Deliberately reproduce and repair one test-visible defect.

Finish README prerequisites, setup, exact commands, tests, data behavior, structure, known limits, and evidence. Copy the supplied .gitignore and replace the data file with `[]` or a sanitized sample.

Initialize Git, make meaningful commits, create a free GitHub repository, inspect `git status --short` before and after `git add .`, remove any secret/private/cache path from staging, push normally, and follow the README from a fresh folder view before proof.

templates.label: Exact command and result contract
templates.content:
# Record
{id: int, title: str, course: str, status: "open" | "done"}
- First ID 1; later ID highest existing + 1.

# Commands
py -m tasktrail.cli add "Finish lab" --course "CSC 101"
  -> Added task #1.
py -m tasktrail.cli list
  -> #1 [OPEN] Finish lab | CSC 101, or: No tasks found.
py -m tasktrail.cli list --status done
  -> matching lines, or: No tasks found.
py -m tasktrail.cli complete 1
  -> Completed task #1.
py -m tasktrail.cli --help
  -> argparse usage and subcommands.

# Exact domain errors
blank title -> ValueError("title must not be blank")
blank course -> ValueError("course must not be blank")
unknown ID -> LookupError(f"task #{task_id} was not found")
repeated complete -> ValueError(f"task #{task_id} is already done")
